section_title: How does Jesus tell us to stay ready?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 34 But watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life—and that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare. 35 For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth. 36 So keep watch at all times, and pray that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.”
37 Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. 38 And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple.

context_lines: Jesus concludes by calling His followers to watch themselves. He names excess, drunkenness and the worries of life as things that weigh down the heart, leaving people unprepared when the day arrives.

His response is watchfulness and prayer for strength to escape what is coming and stand before the Son of Man. The teaching directs His followers toward a way of living and depending on God while they wait.

Luke closes the chapter by describing Jesus’ pattern: teaching in the temple during the day, spending the night on the Mount of Olives and being heard by people who come early in the morning. The final teaching takes place within His continuing ministry as the Passover approaches.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings commonly understand these verses as a call to spiritual alertness, prayer and a life that is ready to meet the Lord. Wesley takes the warning seriously even for established believers and describes watchfulness as the conclusion of the teaching; the following summary emphasizes listening to Jesus’ instruction. ([Wesley on Luke 21:34–38](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-luke/))
god_plan_lines: First Thessalonians connects wakefulness and sobriety with faith, love and hope, grounding that hope in Christ’s death so that His people may live with Him. The waiting community is called to encourage and build up one another. ([1 Thessalonians 5:4–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_thessalonians/5.htm))

First Peter likewise joins sober prayer to deep love, hospitality and using God-given abilities to serve others. These passages show the shared life that grows from readiness: dependence on God becomes care for people, with God glorified through Jesus Christ. ([1 Peter 4:7–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/4.htm))
